| Contractual mechanism | HIPAA requires a business associate contract or qualifying other arrangement that meets specified requirements. **45 CFR §§ 164.504(e)(1), 164.314(a)(1)**. | SOC 2 does not require a named contract type, but vendor commitments are expected where relevant: for confidentiality, the entity obtains confidentiality commitments from vendors/business partners with access to confidential information; for privacy, it obtains privacy commitments consistent with the entity’s privacy commitments and requirements. **SOC 2 TSC CC9.2**. SOC 2 service commitments may also be communicated through contracts, SLAs, or published policies. **SOC 2 Description Criteria DC2 implementation guidance**. |
| Required contract contents | HIPAA contracts must establish permitted and required PHI uses/disclosures and may not authorize uses/disclosures that would violate HIPAA if done by the covered entity, except limited management/administration or data aggregation uses. **45 CFR § 164.504(e)(2)(i)**. They must require the business associate not to use or disclose PHI except as permitted/required by contract or law. **45 CFR § 164.504(e)(2)(ii)(A)**. | SOC 2 does not prescribe exact clauses. It expects controls over vendor/business-partner relationships, including communication and resolution protocols, exception handling procedures, performance assessment, issue remediation, and termination procedures. **SOC 2 TSC CC9.2**. |
| Safeguards | HIPAA contracts must require the business associate to use appropriate safeguards and, for ePHI, comply where applicable with the HIPAA Security Rule to prevent unauthorized uses/disclosures. **45 CFR § 164.504(e)(2)(ii)(B)**. Security Rule business associate contracts must require compliance with applicable Security Rule requirements. **45 CFR § 164.314(a)(2)(i)(A)**. | SOC 2 addresses safeguards through the selected Trust Services Criteria and the entity’s system controls; vendor-related risk must be considered in risk assessment and managed through vendor controls. **SOC 2 TSC CC3.2, CC9.2**. Where subservice controls are necessary, the SOC 2 description must identify the subservice organization’s role and the controls assumed or included, depending on report method. **SOC 2 Description Criteria DC7**. |
| Flow-down to subcontractors | HIPAA requires the business associate to ensure subcontractors that create, receive, maintain, or transmit PHI agree to the same restrictions and conditions that apply to the business associate. **45 CFR § 164.504(e)(2)(ii)(D)**. For ePHI, the business associate must ensure subcontractors agree to comply with applicable Security Rule requirements through a contract or arrangement. **45 CFR § 164.314(a)(2)(i)(B), § 164.314(a)(2)(iii)**. | SOC 2 handles downstream/vendor controls through the concept of subservice organizations and complementary subservice organization controls. If using the carve-out method, the description identifies the applicable criteria intended to be met by subservice controls and the types of controls assumed to be implemented by the subservice organization. **SOC 2 Description Criteria DC7**. |
| Incident / breach reporting | HIPAA contracts must require the business associate to report to the covered entity uses/disclosures not provided for by the contract, including breaches of unsecured PHI. **45 CFR § 164.504(e)(2)(ii)(C)**. Security Rule contracts must require reporting of any security incident of which the business associate becomes aware, including breaches of unsecured PHI as required by § 164.410. **45 CFR § 164.314(a)(2)(i)(C)**. | SOC 2 does not prescribe HIPAA-style breach notification terms, but vendor issue communication and resolution protocols and exception-handling procedures are points of focus under vendor risk management. **SOC 2 TSC CC9.2**. SOC 2 descriptions may also need to disclose significant system incidents, including incidents involving unauthorized use or disclosure of sensitive information such as personal health information. **SOC 2 Description Criteria DC4 implementation guidance**. |
| Ongoing oversight | HIPAA’s explicit oversight trigger is knowledge-based: a covered entity is not compliant if it knew of a pattern of activity or practice constituting a material breach/violation unless it took reasonable steps to cure or end the violation and, if unsuccessful, terminated the contract if feasible. **45 CFR § 164.504(e)(1)(ii)**. The same rule applies to a business associate that knows of a subcontractor’s material breach/violation. **45 CFR § 164.504(e)(1)(iii)**. HIPAA does not, in these cited provisions, prescribe a general periodic vendor audit cadence. | SOC 2 is more explicit about routine, risk-based oversight: the entity assesses vendor and business partner performance as frequently as warranted based on vendor/business-partner risk, assesses compliance with confidentiality commitments periodically and as needed, and implements procedures for addressing issues found in vendor assessments. **SOC 2 TSC CC9.2**. |
| Access, amendment, accounting support | HIPAA contracts must require the business associate to make PHI available for individual access, amendment, and accounting of disclosures where applicable. **45 CFR § 164.504(e)(2)(ii)(E)–(G)**. | SOC 2 has no direct equivalent unless those obligations are part of the organization’s service commitments/system requirements or selected privacy criteria. SOC 2 evaluates controls against selected criteria and commitments, rather than imposing HIPAA-style individual-rights clauses. **SOC 2 Description Criteria DC2; SOC 2 TSC CC9.2 privacy points of focus**. |
| Regulator / auditor access | HIPAA contracts must require the business associate to make internal practices, books, and records relating to PHI available to the Secretary of HHS to determine the covered entity’s compliance. **45 CFR § 164.504(e)(2)(ii)(I)**. Business associates must also disclose PHI to the Secretary when required for compliance investigations. **45 CFR § 164.502(a)(4)(i)**. | SOC 2 does not create HHS-style regulator access obligations. Instead, management’s SOC 2 description and controls are examined by a service auditor, and the report describes controls and, for Type 2, their operating effectiveness. **SOC 2 Description Criteria introductory guidance; SOC 2 definition of SOC 2 examination**. |
| Termination / exit | HIPAA contracts must authorize the covered entity to terminate the contract if it determines the business associate violated a material term. **45 CFR § 164.504(e)(2)(iii)**. On termination, the business associate must return or destroy PHI if feasible, retain no copies, or extend contract protections and limit further uses/disclosures if return/destruction is infeasible. **45 CFR § 164.504(e)(2)(ii)(J)**. | SOC 2 expects procedures for terminating vendor/business-partner relationships based on predefined considerations; those procedures may include safe return of data and removal from the vendor/business-partner system. **SOC 2 TSC CC9.2**. |
| Nature of obligation | HIPAA’s vendor obligations are legal requirements in the Privacy and Security Rules, with specified contract terms and defined compliance consequences. **45 CFR §§ 164.502(e), 164.504(e), 164.314(a)**. | SOC 2’s vendor obligations are control criteria and points of focus used to evaluate whether controls are suitably designed and operating effectively to meet service commitments and system requirements. **SOC 2 TSC CC3.2, CC3.4, CC9.2; SOC 2 Description Criteria DC7**. |

---

## Key practical differences

1. **HIPAA requires a BAA-style legal instrument; SOC 2 requires risk-based controls and evidence.**  
   HIPAA requires satisfactory assurances through a business associate contract or other qualifying arrangement before PHI/ePHI is handled by a business associate. **45 CFR §§ 164.502(e)(1), 164.504(e), 164.314(a)**. SOC 2 instead evaluates whether the organization identifies vendor risks, manages vendor performance, obtains relevant confidentiality/privacy commitments, handles issues, and terminates vendors appropriately. **SOC 2 TSC CC3.2, CC3.4, CC9.2**.

2. **HIPAA contract clauses are highly specific.**  
   HIPAA specifies clauses on permitted uses/disclosures, safeguards, breach/security-incident reporting, subcontractor flow-down, individual access/amendment/accounting support, compliance with delegated covered-entity obligations, HHS access, return/destruction of PHI, and termination rights. **45 CFR § 164.504(e)(2)(i)–(iii); § 164.314(a)(2)**.

3. **SOC 2 oversight is more continuous and risk-calibrated.**  
   SOC 2 expressly expects vendor/business-partner performance assessment “as frequently as warranted” based on risk, issue remediation, exception handling, and termination procedures. **SOC 2 TSC CC9.2**. HIPAA’s cited oversight obligation is more focused on obtaining assurances and responding when the entity knows of a material breach or violation. **45 CFR § 164.504(e)(1)(ii)–(iii)**.

4. **SOC 2 has a reporting/scoping concept HIPAA does not.**  
   In SOC 2, if a vendor’s controls are necessary to meet the service organization’s commitments, the vendor may be a subservice organization; management must decide whether to use the inclusive or carve-out method and disclose the nature of the subservice services, relevant controls or assumed controls, and complementary subservice organization controls as applicable. **SOC 2 Description Criteria DC7**. HIPAA does not use SOC 2-style inclusive/carve-out reporting; it uses business associate and subcontractor contract obligations. **45 CFR §§ 160.103, 164.502(e), 164.504(e), 164.314(a)**.

5. **HIPAA is PHI-specific; SOC 2 depends on scope and selected categories.**  
   HIPAA vendor obligations attach to PHI/ePHI handled by business associates and subcontractors. **45 CFR §§ 160.103, 164.502(e)**. SOC 2 vendor obligations are evaluated relative to the service organization’s selected Trust Services Categories and its service commitments/system requirements, such as security, availability, confidentiality, or privacy. **SOC 2 Description Criteria DC2; SOC 2 TSC CC9.2**.

scores.judge_rationale: The candidate answer fully and accurately captures the core comparison: HIPAA's prescriptive BAA requirements with specific contract clauses versus SOC 2's risk-based, non-prescriptive approach to vendor management, and correctly cites all expected regulations (SOC 2 CC9.2; HIPAA §§164.502(e), 164.504(e), 164.314(a)) plus additional relevant sections that enhance rather than detract from the answer.

question.question: Compare the governance expectations in NIST AI RMF's GOVERN function with the quality management system requirements in EU AI Act Article 17 for high-risk AI system providers.
question.expected_answer: NIST AI RMF GOVERN prescribes organisation-wide structures, policies, accountability, roles, transparency, workforce competence, supplier oversight, and engagement with affected stakeholders — non-binding. EU AI Act Article 17 requires providers of high-risk AI systems to have a QMS that includes: regulatory compliance strategy, design control, technical specifications, quality control techniques, data management, risk management (Article 9), post-market monitoring (Article 72), incident reporting (Article 73), communication with authorities, record-keeping, and resource management — binding and auditable for conformity assessment.
question.notes: Governance vs QMS comparison; one is voluntary, one is auditable for CE marking.

output.answer:
## Bottom line

NIST AI RMF’s **GOVERN** function and EU AI Act **Article 17** both expect an organization-wide governance system with documented policies, defined accountability, risk management, testing/monitoring, and lifecycle controls. The key difference is that **NIST GOVERN is a flexible, cross-cutting AI risk-governance framework**, while **EU AI Act Article 17 is a mandatory, provider-focused quality management system (QMS) requirement for high-risk AI systems**. NIST is broader on culture, trustworthy AI, stakeholder engagement, diversity, and third-party risk; Article 17 is more prescriptive on regulatory compliance, conformity assessment, design/development controls, data management, post-market monitoring, incident reporting, recordkeeping, and communications with authorities.

## Side-by-side comparison

| Topic | NIST AI RMF GOVERN | EU AI Act Article 17 QMS |
|---|---|---|
| Legal character | GOVERN is framed as a risk-management function that “enables” the other AI RMF functions and should be integrated across AI risk management over the AI system lifecycle and organizational hierarchy. (NIST AI RMF 1.0, §5.1 “Govern”) | Providers of high-risk AI systems “shall put a quality management system in place” that ensures compliance with the Regulation. (EU AI Act, Art. 17(1)); providers are separately obligated to have a QMS that complies with Art. 17. (EU AI Act, Art. 16(c)) |
| Overall purpose | GOVERN aims to cultivate a risk-management culture, align AI risk management with organizational principles and strategic priorities, connect technical AI work to organizational values, and address the full product lifecycle including third-party software, hardware, and data. (NIST AI RMF 1.0, §5.1 “Govern”) | Article 17 aims to ensure legal compliance for high-risk AI systems through a documented QMS covering regulatory strategy, design/development controls, testing, standards, data management, risk management, post-market monitoring, incident reporting, recordkeeping, resources, and accountability. (EU AI Act, Art. 17(1)(a)–(m)) |
| Documentation | GOVERN expects policies, processes, procedures, and practices for mapping, measuring, and managing AI risks to be in place, transparent, and effectively implemented. (NIST AI RMF 1.0, GOVERN 1) | The QMS must be documented “in a systematic and orderly manner” through written policies, procedures, and instructions. (EU AI Act, Art. 17(1)) |
| Regulatory compliance | GOVERN expects legal and regulatory requirements involving AI to be understood, managed, and documented. (NIST AI RMF 1.0, GOVERN 1.1) | Article 17 requires a regulatory compliance strategy, including compliance with conformity assessment procedures and procedures for managing modifications to the high-risk AI system. (EU AI Act, Art. 17(1)(a)) |
| Risk management | GOVERN requires risk-management processes and outcomes to be established through transparent policies and controls based on organizational risk priorities, with monitoring and periodic review. (NIST AI RMF 1.0, GOVERN 1.4–1.5) | Article 17 requires the QMS to include the risk management system referred to in Article 9. (EU AI Act, Art. 17(1)(g)); Article 9 requires the risk management system to be established, implemented, documented, maintained, and run as a continuous iterative lifecycle process. (EU AI Act, Art. 9(1)–(2)) |
| Accountability | GOVERN requires documented roles, responsibilities, and communication lines for mapping, measuring, and managing AI risks, and it states that executive leadership takes responsibility for decisions about AI-system development and deployment risks. (NIST AI RMF 1.0, GOVERN 2.1, 2.3) | Article 17 requires an accountability framework setting out responsibilities of management and other staff for all listed QMS aspects. (EU AI Act, Art. 17(1)(m)) |
| Training | GOVERN expects personnel and partners to receive AI risk-management training consistent with policies, procedures, and agreements. (NIST AI RMF 1.0, GOVERN 2.2) | Article 17 does not list training as a standalone QMS element, but Article 9 requires, where appropriate, provision of information and training to deployers as part of risk-management measures. (EU AI Act, Art. 9(5)(c)) |
| Testing, validation, and monitoring | GOVERN expects practices for AI testing, incident identification, and information sharing. (NIST AI RMF 1.0, GOVERN 4.3); NIST also emphasizes test, evaluation, verification, and validation across the AI lifecycle. (NIST AI RMF 1.0, §2 “Audience” and §5.1 “Govern”) | Article 17 explicitly requires examination, test, and validation procedures before, during, and after development, including their frequency. (EU AI Act, Art. 17(1)(d)); it also requires post-market monitoring in accordance with Article 72. (EU AI Act, Art. 17(1)(h)) |
| Design and development controls | GOVERN is principle/process-oriented and expects organizational policies and procedures for AI risk mapping, measuring, and managing. (NIST AI RMF 1.0, GOVERN 1) | Article 17 is more specific: the QMS must cover design, design control, design verification, development, quality control, and quality assurance techniques and systematic actions. (EU AI Act, Art. 17(1)(b)–(c)) |
| Data governance | GOVERN addresses full lifecycle issues, including third-party data and other supply chain issues. (NIST AI RMF 1.0, §5.1 “Govern”; GOVERN 6) | Article 17 expressly requires systems and procedures for data acquisition, collection, analysis, labelling, storage, filtration, mining, aggregation, retention, and other data operations before and for placing on the market or putting into service. (EU AI Act, Art. 17(1)(f)) |
| Standards and technical specifications | GOVERN does not prescribe harmonised standards but expects risk processes to align with legal, regulatory, organizational, domain, sector, and professional requirements. (NIST AI RMF 1.0, GOVERN 1.1; §1.2.2 “Risk Tolerance”) | Article 17 requires technical specifications, including standards, and requires providers to specify how compliance will be ensured where harmonised standards are not fully applied or do not cover all relevant requirements. (EU AI Act, Art. 17(1)(e)) |
| Incident handling | GOVERN expects organizational practices for incident identification and information sharing, and contingency processes for failures or incidents in high-risk third-party data or AI systems. (NIST AI RMF 1.0, GOVERN 4.3, 6.2) | Article 17 requires procedures for reporting serious incidents in accordance with Article 73. (EU AI Act, Art. 17(1)(i)) |
| Stakeholder / external engagement | GOVERN requires robust engagement with relevant AI actors, including collecting, considering, prioritizing, and integrating feedback from outside the development or deployment team on individual and societal impacts. (NIST AI RMF 1.0, GOVERN 5.1–5.2) | Article 17 requires handling communications with national competent authorities, other relevant authorities, notified bodies, other operators, customers, and other interested parties. (EU AI Act, Art. 17(1)(j)) |
| Diversity, equity, inclusion, accessibility | GOVERN expressly prioritizes workforce diversity, equity, inclusion, and accessibility in AI risk mapping, measuring, and management, including diverse decision-making teams. (NIST AI RMF 1.0, GOVERN 3.1) | Article 17 does not contain an equivalent DEIA governance requirement, although high-risk providers must ensure accessibility compliance under separate provider obligations. (EU AI Act, Art. 16(l)) |
| Inventory and decommissioning | GOVERN calls for mechanisms to inventory AI systems and for processes to decommission or phase out AI systems safely without increasing risks or decreasing trustworthiness. (NIST AI RMF 1.0, GOVERN 1.6–1.7) | Article 17 does not use the same inventory/decommissioning framing, but it requires modification-management procedures, post-market monitoring, incident reporting, recordkeeping, and resource management. (EU AI Act, Art. 17(1)(a), (h), (i), (k), (l)) |
| Third-party and supply-chain risk | GOVERN expressly requires policies and procedures for AI risks and benefits arising from third-party software, data, and supply-chain issues, including intellectual-property and rights risks, and contingency processes for high-risk third-party failures or incidents. (NIST AI RMF 1.0, GOVERN 6.1–6.2) | Article 17 addresses supply-chain-like concerns through resource management, communications with other operators and interested parties, data management, and standards/technical specifications, but it is less explicit than NIST GOVERN on third-party AI/data risk governance. (EU AI Act, Art. 17(1)(e), (f), (j), (l)) |
| Proportionality | NIST notes that organizations may apply the AI RMF functions based on their resources and capabilities and may select categories/subcategories according to need. (NIST AI RMF 1.0, §5.1 introductory text) | Article 17 allows implementation of QMS aspects to be proportionate to the provider’s size, but providers must still respect the degree of rigour and protection required for compliance of high-risk AI systems. (EU AI Act, Art. 17(2)) |

## Practical interpretation

For an organization already implementing NIST AI RMF GOVERN, the strongest overlap with Article 17 is in **documented governance, accountability, lifecycle risk management, monitoring, testing, incident processes, third-party controls, and feedback/communication mechanisms**. These map most directly to NIST GOVERN 1, 2, 4, 5, and 6 and EU AI Act Article 17(1)(a), (d), (g), (h), (i), (j), (k), and (m). (NIST AI RMF 1.0, GOVERN 1–2 and 4–6; EU AI Act, Art. 17(1)(a), (d), (g)–(m))

However, NIST GOVERN alone would not be enough to evidence Article 17 compliance unless it is supplemented with the EU AI Act’s specific QMS artifacts: conformity-assessment strategy, design control and verification procedures, development QA/QC procedures, defined validation frequencies, harmonised-standard or alternative-compliance analysis, detailed data-management procedures, Article 9 risk-management documentation, Article 72 post-market monitoring, Article 73 serious-incident reporting procedures, and recordkeeping systems. (EU AI Act, Art. 17(1)(a)–(m); EU AI Act, Art. 9(1)–(2))

Conversely, an Article 17 QMS may satisfy many structural governance expectations in NIST GOVERN, but it may be thinner than NIST on **risk culture, trustworthy-AI principles, diverse and multidisciplinary decision-making, societal-impact feedback loops, and explicit third-party AI/data contingency planning**. (NIST AI RMF 1.0, §5.1 “Govern”; GOVERN 1.2, 3.1, 4.1–4.3, 5.1–5.2, 6.1–6.2)

scores.judge_rationale: The candidate answer comprehensively and accurately compares both frameworks, correctly identifying NIST GOVERN's non-binding, culture-focused approach versus Article 17's binding, prescriptive QMS requirements, with precise citations to NIST AI RMF §5/GOVERN subcategories and EU AI Act Article 17(1)(a)-(m) plus cross-referenced Articles 9, 16, 72, and 73.

question.question: For ongoing performance monitoring of production models, compare what SR 11-7 expects of a bank with what NIST AI RMF's MEASURE function recommends.
question.expected_answer: SR 11-7 requires ongoing monitoring of model performance after deployment, including process verification, benchmarking, sensitivity analysis, and outcomes analysis against actual performance. Monitoring frequency must reflect the model's risk tier and changes in use, inputs, or environment; thresholds and escalation procedures must be defined. NIST AI RMF MEASURE includes Sub-categories on continuous tracking of identified risks (MEASURE 2 / 3 / 4) over time and feedback to MANAGE, with explicit treatment of drift, distributional shift, and emergent risks; metrics, owners, and review cadence are expected.

output.answer:
Below is a comparison focused on **ongoing performance monitoring of production models**.

| Topic | SR 11-7 / bank model-risk expectation | NIST AI RMF MEASURE recommendation |
|---|---|---|
| Core objective | A bank should monitor whether a model is **performing as expected** as conditions change, including changes in products, exposures, activities, clients, data relevance, or market conditions. If performance deteriorates, overlays, adjustment, recalibration, or redevelopment may be warranted. **[SR 11-7, Model Validation and Monitoring — Ongoing Model Monitoring]** | Organizations should use quantitative, qualitative, or mixed methods to **analyze, assess, benchmark, and monitor AI risk and impacts**, and AI systems should be tested before deployment and regularly while in operation. **[NIST AI RMF 1.0, §5.3 MEASURE]** |
| Performance against real outcomes | SR 11-7 emphasizes **outcomes analysis**: comparing model outputs to corresponding real-world outcomes to assess performance relative to model objectives and business use. **[SR 11-7, Model Validation and Monitoring — Outcomes Analysis]** | NIST also calls for measuring AI system performance or assurance criteria qualitatively or quantitatively under conditions similar to deployment settings, with measures documented. **[NIST AI RMF 1.0, MEASURE 2.3]** |
| Production monitoring | SR 11-7 treats ongoing monitoring as part of validation and model-risk management, including monitoring for deterioration and deviations from expected performance. **[SR 11-7, Model Validation and Monitoring]** | NIST explicitly recommends that the **functionality and behavior** of the AI system and its components be monitored when in production. **[NIST AI RMF 1.0, MEASURE 2.4]** |
| Thresholds and remediation | SR 11-7 links monitoring to the bank’s established performance thresholds and says material errors or persistent deviations may warrant model adjustment, recalibration, or redevelopment. **[SR 11-7, Model Validation and Monitoring — Outcomes Analysis; Ongoing Model Monitoring]** | NIST says measurement should support management decisions such as recalibration, impact mitigation, removal from production or use, and compensating or recovery controls. **[NIST AI RMF 1.0, §5.3 MEASURE]** |
| Model limitations | SR 11-7 expects ongoing monitoring plans to include regular assessment of model limitations identified at development and over time, plus procedures for responding to issues before and after approval for use. **[SR 11-7, Model Validation and Monitoring — Ongoing Model Monitoring]** | NIST recommends documenting limitations of generalizability beyond the conditions under which the technology was developed. **[NIST AI RMF 1.0, MEASURE 2.5]** |
| Independence / challenge | SR 11-7 expects “effective challenge” by objective experts with appropriate expertise, independence, and organizational standing across the model lifecycle, including ongoing monitoring. **[SR 11-7, Overview of Model Risk and Model Risk Management]** | NIST recommends involving internal experts who were not front-line developers and/or independent assessors in regular assessments and updates; it also recommends consulting domain experts, users, external AI actors, and affected communities as needed. **[NIST AI RMF 1.0, MEASURE 1.3]** |
| Metrics and documentation | SR 11-7 expects monitoring and validation to evaluate reliability, limitations, and whether corrective action may be warranted, with rigor aligned to model approach, use, and materiality. **[SR 11-7, Model Validation and Monitoring]** | NIST is more explicit about documenting test sets, metrics, tools, TEVV methods, performance measures, and the effectiveness of measurement processes. **[NIST AI RMF 1.0, MEASURE 2.1; MEASURE 2.13]** |
| Risk scope | SR 11-7 is bank model-risk focused: model risk is the potential for adverse financial consequences from decisions based on model output, and monitoring is tied to business use, model purpose, and banking risk. **[SR 11-7, Overview of Model Risk and Model Risk Management]** | NIST’s MEASURE function covers broader AI trustworthiness risks, including safety, security and resilience, transparency and accountability, privacy, fairness and bias, environmental impact, and emergent risks. **[NIST AI RMF 1.0, MEASURE 2.6–2.12; MEASURE 3.1]** |
| Emergent and unanticipated risks | SR 11-7 expects monitoring to account for changing conditions and performance deterioration over time. **[SR 11-7, Model Validation and Monitoring — Ongoing Model Monitoring]** | NIST specifically recommends mechanisms to regularly identify and track existing, unanticipated, and emergent AI risks based on intended and actual performance in deployed contexts. **[NIST AI RMF 1.0, MEASURE 3.1]** |

### Bottom line

For a bank, **SR 11-7 is more prescriptive in a model-risk-management sense**: production monitoring should determine whether the model continues to perform as intended for its approved business use, compare outputs to outcomes where possible, detect deviations from thresholds, reassess limitations, and trigger overlays, recalibration, adjustment, or redevelopment when warranted. **[SR 11-7, Model Validation and Monitoring — Outcomes Analysis; Ongoing Model Monitoring]**

The **NIST AI RMF MEASURE function is broader and more AI-trustworthiness oriented**: it recommends ongoing production monitoring plus documented metrics, TEVV practices, independent review, tracking of emergent risks, and measurement of trustworthiness dimensions such as safety, security, privacy, fairness, transparency, accountability, and environmental impact. **[NIST AI RMF 1.0, §5.3 MEASURE; MEASURE 1.1–1.3; MEASURE 2.1–2.13; MEASURE 3.1–3.2]**

In practice, a bank using AI models would likely need **both**: SR 11-7-style monitoring for model performance, business use, outcomes, thresholds, and remediation, plus NIST-style measurement for broader AI risks and trustworthiness attributes that traditional model monitoring may not fully cover. **[SR 11-7, Model Validation and Monitoring; NIST AI RMF 1.0, §5.3 MEASURE]**

scores.judge_rationale: The answer is comprehensive and accurate in capturing SR 11-7's ongoing monitoring requirements and NIST AI RMF MEASURE's broader trustworthiness focus, but citations are partially incorrect: SR 11-7 uses 'Section IV. Ongoing Monitoring' not 'Model Validation and Monitoring' as section headers, and while NIST MEASURE 2.4, 2.5, 3.1 are valid, the expected citations MEASURE 2.x and 3.x are broadly met though not precisely as specified; the SR 11-7 citations deviate from expected section naming convention.

question.question: What did HHS propose changing in the 2024 NPRM to the HIPAA Security Rule compared to the rule as it stood after the 2013 Omnibus Rule?
question.expected_answer: The 2024 NPRM proposes substantial modernisation: removal of the 'addressable' vs 'required' distinction (making most specifications required), explicit written documentation requirements for risk analysis and risk management, mandatory encryption of ePHI at rest and in transit with limited exceptions, multi-factor authentication, vulnerability scanning and penetration testing on defined cadences, network segmentation, and stricter business-associate oversight. The 2013 Omnibus version retained 'addressable' implementation specifications and did not require MFA, scanning, or pen testing.
question.notes: Edition-aware: naive cannot filter to 2024 vs 2013 and tends to conflate.

output.answer:
HHS’s 2024 HIPAA Security Rule NPRM would not merely “update” the 2013 Omnibus Rule; it would substantially make the Security Rule more prescriptive. The 2013 Omnibus Rule left the core Security Rule structure largely intact—flexible, risk-based, and with many “addressable” implementation specifications—while extending direct Security Rule obligations to business associates and subcontractors. The NPRM would keep the rule risk-based but add mandatory, specific cybersecurity controls and documentation requirements.  
Sources: current/post-Omnibus Security Rule at 45 CFR §§ 164.302, 164.306, 164.308, 164.310, 164.312, 164.314, 164.316; HHS/OCR NPRM, *HIPAA Security Rule to Strengthen the Cybersecurity of Electronic Protected Health Information*, 90 Fed. Reg. 898 (Jan. 6, 2025), https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2025/01/06/2024-30983/hipaa-security-rule-to-strengthen-the-cybersecurity-of-electronic-protected-health-information.

| Topic | Rule as it stood after 2013 Omnibus | What HHS proposed in the 2024 NPRM |
|---|---|---|
| **Who must comply** | Covered entities and business associates must comply with Security Rule standards for ePHI. The Omnibus Rule made business associates directly subject to the applicable Security Rule requirements. 45 CFR §§ 164.302, 164.104(b). | HHS would keep covered entities and business associates within scope, but impose more specific assurance obligations between covered entities, business associates, and subcontractors, including written verification/certification of technical safeguard deployment. NPRM proposed §§ 164.308, 164.314. |
| **Required vs. addressable safeguards** | The rule distinguished “required” and “addressable” implementation specifications. For addressable items, a regulated entity could implement the specification, document why it was not reasonable and appropriate, and implement an equivalent alternative if reasonable and appropriate. 45 CFR § 164.306(d). | HHS proposed eliminating the “addressable” category and making implementation specifications mandatory, subject only to limited exceptions that would have to be documented. NPRM proposed § 164.306. This is one of the biggest structural changes. |
| **Flexibility of approach** | Regulated entities may use any security measures that reasonably and appropriately implement the standards, considering size, complexity, capabilities, technical infrastructure, cost, and risk. 45 CFR § 164.306(b). | The NPRM would preserve scalability/risk-based implementation but pair it with more prescriptive minimum controls—e.g., encryption, MFA, inventories, vulnerability scanning, and testing—rather than leaving many controls as addressable. NPRM proposed §§ 164.306, 164.308, 164.312. |
| **Risk analysis** | Current rule requires an “accurate and thorough assessment” of risks and vulnerabilities to ePHI confidentiality, integrity, and availability. 45 CFR § 164.308(a)(1)(ii)(A). | HHS proposed specifying what the risk analysis must include, such as a written assessment, review of technology assets, network maps, ePHI movement, reasonably anticipated threats and vulnerabilities, likelihood/impact, and risk levels. NPRM proposed § 164.308(a)(1). |
| **Asset inventory and network map** | No express requirement to maintain a technology asset inventory or network map, although entities must conduct risk analysis and maintain documentation. 45 CFR §§ 164.308(a)(1)(ii)(A), 164.316(b). | HHS proposed requiring a written technology asset inventory and network map showing relevant electronic information systems and movement of ePHI, updated at least annually and after changes affecting ePHI. NPRM proposed § 164.308. |
| **Risk management** | Entities must implement security measures sufficient to reduce risks and vulnerabilities to a reasonable and appropriate level. 45 CFR § 164.308(a)(1)(ii)(B). | HHS proposed more detailed written risk-management requirements, including documented risk-management planning and implementation of measures to address identified risks. NPRM proposed § 164.308(a)(1). |
| **Security evaluation / audits** | Current rule requires periodic technical and nontechnical evaluation in response to environmental or operational changes affecting ePHI security. 45 CFR § 164.308(a)(8). | HHS proposed more explicit, regular compliance-audit/evaluation obligations, including written documentation and periodic review of Security Rule compliance. NPRM proposed § 164.308. |
| **Vulnerability management** | Current rule does not expressly require vulnerability scanning or penetration testing, although these may be reasonable safeguards under risk analysis, risk management, and evaluation. 45 CFR §§ 164.308(a)(1), 164.308(a)(8). | HHS proposed requiring vulnerability scanning at least every six months and after relevant changes, plus penetration testing at least annually. NPRM proposed § 164.308. |
| **Patch management** | Current rule does not contain a specific patch-management standard; patching is handled through general risk management, malicious software protection, and system activity review. 45 CFR §§ 164.308(a)(1), 164.308(a)(5), 164.308(a)(8). | HHS proposed specific patch-management obligations as part of strengthened risk management and vulnerability management. NPRM proposed § 164.308. |
| **Security awareness and training** | Entities must implement a security awareness and training program; specific items such as security reminders, malicious software protection, log-in monitoring, and password management are addressable. 45 CFR § 164.308(a)(5). | HHS proposed making training and related implementation specifications mandatory and more specific, including workforce training tied to security risks and operational changes. NPRM proposed § 164.308(a)(5). |
| **Incident response** | Entities must have policies and procedures to address security incidents, identify/respond to incidents, mitigate harmful effects, and document incidents and outcomes. 45 CFR § 164.308(a)(6). | HHS proposed more detailed written security incident response planning, documentation, and response procedures. It also proposed requiring business associates to notify covered entities, and subcontractors to notify business associates, within specified timeframes in some circumstances such as contingency plan activation. NPRM proposed §§ 164.308, 164.314. |
| **Contingency planning / backups** | Current rule requires a contingency plan, including data backup plan, disaster recovery plan, and emergency mode operation plan; testing/revision and applications/data criticality analysis are addressable. 45 CFR § 164.308(a)(7). | HHS proposed strengthening contingency planning, making formerly addressable items mandatory, requiring written plans and testing, and adding more concrete expectations for backup/recovery resilience. NPRM proposed § 164.308(a)(7). |
| **Facility and physical safeguards** | Facility access-control implementation specifications—contingency operations, facility security plan, access control/validation, and maintenance records—are addressable; workstation use/security and disposal/media reuse have required elements. 45 CFR § 164.310. | HHS proposed making physical safeguard implementation specifications mandatory and more explicitly documented, consistent with eliminating the addressable/required distinction. NPRM proposed § 164.310. |
| **Access controls** | Current technical access controls require unique user identification and emergency access procedures; automatic logoff and encryption/decryption are addressable. 45 CFR § 164.312(a). | HHS proposed stronger access controls, including mandatory multi-factor authentication for access to ePHI systems, subject to limited exceptions. NPRM proposed § 164.312(a). |
| **Encryption at rest and in transit** | Encryption/decryption for stored ePHI is addressable under access control, and transmission encryption is addressable when deemed appropriate. 45 CFR §§ 164.312(a)(2)(iv), 164.312(e)(2)(ii). | HHS proposed requiring encryption of ePHI at rest and in transit, with limited exceptions that must be documented. NPRM proposed § 164.312. |
| **Audit controls and activity review** | Entities must implement audit controls for systems containing or using ePHI and must regularly review records such as audit logs, access reports, and incident tracking reports. 45 CFR §§ 164.312(b), 164.308(a)(1)(ii)(D). | HHS proposed more specific audit-log and monitoring expectations, including technical controls and written procedures for recording and examining activity in relevant systems. NPRM proposed §§ 164.308, 164.312. |
| **Integrity controls** | Entities must protect ePHI from improper alteration or destruction; mechanisms to authenticate ePHI are addressable. 45 CFR § 164.312(c). | HHS proposed making integrity-related technical controls mandatory rather than addressable, consistent with the broader elimination of addressable specifications. NPRM proposed § 164.312(c). |
| **Transmission security** | Current rule requires technical security measures to guard against unauthorized access to ePHI transmitted over electronic networks; integrity controls and encryption are addressable. 45 CFR § 164.312(e). | HHS proposed mandatory transmission security controls, including encryption of ePHI in transit, subject to limited documented exceptions. NPRM proposed § 164.312(e). |
| **Business associate contracts and assurances** | Business associate contracts must require the BA to comply with applicable Security Rule requirements, ensure subcontractors agree to comply, and report security incidents and breaches. 45 CFR § 164.314(a)(2). | HHS proposed more specific BA/subcontractor obligations, including written verification to covered entities or upstream BAs that technical safeguards have been deployed, and additional notification obligations. NPRM proposed § 164.314. |
| **Documentation** | Entities must maintain Security Rule policies/procedures in written or electronic form, retain required documentation for six years, make it available to implementers, and update it periodically as needed. 45 CFR § 164.316(b). | HHS proposed expanding and sharpening written-documentation requirements for analyses, inventories, maps, plans, reviews, exceptions, audits, and technical safeguard decisions. NPRM proposed § 164.316. |

**Bottom line:** after the 2013 Omnibus Rule, HIPAA Security Rule compliance remained largely flexible and risk-based, with many “addressable” controls and general standards. The 2024 NPRM would move the rule toward a more prescriptive cybersecurity baseline: mandatory encryption, MFA, asset inventories, network mapping, vulnerability scanning, penetration testing, stronger contingency planning, annual audits/evaluations, and more formal documentation and business-associate assurance requirements.

scores.judge_rationale: The candidate answer comprehensively covers all key changes in the 2024 NPRM compared to the 2013 Omnibus Rule with accurate specificity, and properly cites both the current 45 CFR Part 164 regulations and the 2025 Federal Register NPRM with correct section references throughout.

question.question: What's the substantive difference between NIST AI RMF 1.0 (January 2023) and the earlier 2022 working drafts in terms of trustworthiness characteristics?
question.expected_answer: The final NIST AI RMF 1.0 (Jan 2023) consolidated the trustworthiness characteristics into a set of seven: valid & reliable; safe; secure & resilient; accountable & transparent; explainable & interpretable; privacy-enhanced; and fair (with managed harmful bias). Earlier 2022 drafts treated these as a longer overlapping list with terms like 'enhanced privacy' and 'bias mitigation' that were renamed for clarity, and the GOVERN function was strengthened relative to drafts to emphasise organisation-wide responsibility rather than only the AI team.

output.answer:
The substantive change is that **AI RMF 1.0 converted the 2022 draft taxonomy into a smaller, more integrated set of “trustworthy AI characteristics,” and moved away from treating some items as separate technical metrics or high-level principles.** It did **not** radically introduce a new trustworthiness concept in January 2023; it mostly **consolidated, renamed, reordered, and clarified** the characteristics.

| Version | Treatment of trustworthiness characteristics | Substantive difference |
|---|---|---|
| **Initial Draft 1 / March 2022** | Used a **three-class taxonomy**: **technical characteristics** — accuracy, reliability, robustness, resilience or ML security; **socio-technical characteristics** — explainability, interpretability, privacy, safety, managing bias; and **guiding principles** — fairness, accountability, transparency. | Trustworthiness was framed as a taxonomy separating measurable/technical traits from socio-technical traits and broader principles. Accuracy, robustness, fairness, accountability, and transparency were more distinct standalone items or principles. *(NIST AI RMF 2022 Draft 1, §5, §5.1, §5.2, §5.3)* |
| **Second Draft / August 2022** | Collapsed the taxonomy into seven grouped characteristics: **Valid and Reliable; Safe; Fair – and Bias Is Managed; Secure and Resilient; Transparent and Accountable; Explainable and Interpretable; Privacy-Enhanced.** *(NIST AI RMF 2022 Draft 2, Table of Contents/§4.1–§4.7)* | This draft already moved close to the final structure by folding accuracy and robustness into validity/reliability, combining security with resilience, pairing transparency with accountability, and pairing explainability with interpretability. *(NIST AI RMF 2022 Draft 2, §4.1, §4.4–§4.7)* |
| **AI RMF 1.0 / January 2023** | Final list: **valid and reliable; safe; secure and resilient; accountable and transparent; explainable and interpretable; privacy enhanced; and fair with harmful bias managed.** *(NIST AI RMF 1.0, Part 1/§3; NIST AI 100-1, p. 3)* | Final version largely preserves the second draft’s seven-characteristic structure but changes emphasis: accountability is placed before transparency, fairness is framed as “fair — with harmful bias managed,” and the text stresses tradeoffs among characteristics rather than a strict taxonomy. *(NIST AI RMF 1.0, §3.4, §3.7)* |

Key substantive differences:

1. **Accuracy and robustness stopped being standalone trustworthiness characteristics.**  
   In Draft 1, **accuracy**, **reliability**, and **robustness** were separate technical characteristics. *(NIST AI RMF 2022 Draft 1, §5.1.1–§5.1.3)* In Draft 2 and AI RMF 1.0, accuracy and robustness/generalizability are treated as contributors to **validity and reliability**, rather than separate headline characteristics. *(NIST AI RMF 2022 Draft 2, §4.1; NIST AI RMF 1.0, §3.1)*

2. **Security/resilience became a broader AI-system characteristic, not just “ML security.”**  
   Draft 1 used “**Resilience or ML Security**” and focused on adversarial attacks, unexpected changes, and model/data exfiltration. *(NIST AI RMF 2022 Draft 1, §5.1.4)* AI RMF 1.0 uses **“Secure and Resilient”** and clarifies that security and resilience are related but distinct: resilience is the ability to withstand or recover from adverse events, while security also includes protection, response, and recovery from attacks. *(NIST AI RMF 1.0, §3.3)*

3. **Fairness and bias were merged more explicitly.**  
   Draft 1 treated **managing bias** as a socio-technical characteristic and **fairness** as a guiding principle. *(NIST AI RMF 2022 Draft 1, §5.2.5, §5.3.1)* Draft 2 combined them as **“Fair – and Bias Is Managed.”** *(NIST AI RMF 2022 Draft 2, §4.3)* AI RMF 1.0 refines this to **“Fair – with Harmful Bias Managed,”** emphasizing that mitigating harmful bias is necessary but not always sufficient for fairness. *(NIST AI RMF 1.0, §3.7)*

4. **Accountability and transparency were elevated from “guiding principles” into core characteristics.**  
   Draft 1 listed **accountability** and **transparency** as guiding principles. *(NIST AI RMF 2022 Draft 1, §5.3.2–§5.3.3)* Draft 2 grouped them as **“Transparent and Accountable.”** *(NIST AI RMF 2022 Draft 2, §4.5)* AI RMF 1.0 reverses the label to **“Accountable and Transparent”** and states that trustworthy AI depends on accountability and that accountability presupposes transparency. *(NIST AI RMF 1.0, §3.4)*

5. **Explainability and interpretability remained paired, but the final version distinguishes them more cleanly from transparency.**  
   Draft 1 treated explainability and interpretability as separate socio-technical characteristics. *(NIST AI RMF 2022 Draft 1, §5.2.1–§5.2.2)* Draft 2 and AI RMF 1.0 pair them as **“Explainable and Interpretable.”** *(NIST AI RMF 2022 Draft 2, §4.6; NIST AI RMF 1.0, §3.5)* AI RMF 1.0 further distinguishes the concepts: transparency addresses “what happened,” explainability addresses “how” a decision was made, and interpretability addresses “why” it matters in context. *(NIST AI RMF 1.0, §3.5)*

6. **The final version is more explicitly tradeoff-oriented and context-dependent.**  
   Draft 1 already noted that secure-but-unfair, accurate-but-opaque, or inaccurate-but-otherwise-protected systems are undesirable. *(NIST AI RMF 2022 Draft 1, §5.2.5)* AI RMF 1.0 strengthens this point by stating that trustworthiness characteristics influence one another and that risk management requires balancing tradeoffs among them in context. *(NIST AI RMF 1.0, §3, discussion following §3.7)*

Bottom line: **Compared with the March 2022 draft, AI RMF 1.0 substantially reorganized the trustworthiness model from a three-tier taxonomy into seven integrated characteristics. Compared with the August 2022 second draft, the January 2023 final is mostly a refinement: it keeps the seven-characteristic structure but changes emphasis, especially around accountability/transparency and fairness/harmful bias.**

scores.judge_rationale: The candidate answer is fully correct and substantially more detailed than the reference, accurately identifying the consolidation from a three-class taxonomy to seven integrated characteristics, specific renamings (e.g., 'enhanced privacy' to 'privacy-enhanced', 'bias mitigation' to 'fair with harmful bias managed'), and the GOVERN function strengthening is implicitly covered through the accountability/transparency emphasis; citations precisely reference NIST AI RMF 1.0 §3 and 2022 drafts with specific sections.

question.question: What changed between the 2021 Commission proposal for the EU AI Act and the final 2024 text in terms of obligations on general-purpose AI / foundation models?
question.expected_answer: The 2021 proposal did not address general-purpose AI; the final 2024 text added a dedicated chapter (Title VIIIa) on general-purpose AI models with two tiers of obligations: (1) baseline obligations for all GPAI providers — technical documentation, instructions for downstream providers, copyright policy, summary of training data; (2) additional obligations for 'GPAI with systemic risk' (designated by compute threshold or Commission decision) — model evaluations including adversarial testing, systemic-risk assessment and mitigation, serious-incident reporting, cybersecurity, and energy reporting.

output.answer:
Between the **2021 Commission proposal** and the **final 2024 EU AI Act**, the biggest change is that **general-purpose AI / foundation models went from being essentially unaddressed as a standalone regulatory object to being regulated in their own dedicated regime**.

| Issue | 2021 Commission proposal | Final 2024 EU AI Act |
|---|---|---|
| Regulatory concept | No standalone category for “general-purpose AI model” or “foundation model.” The proposal regulated **AI systems** through a risk-based framework. | Introduces “general-purpose AI model” and “general-purpose AI system” definitions, and creates a dedicated regime for them. |
| Scope | Obligations mainly attached to providers/users/importers/distributors of **AI systems**, especially **high-risk AI systems**. | Scope expressly covers providers placing **general-purpose AI models** on the EU market, including non-EU providers. |
| Baseline GPAI obligations | None as such. A foundation model would be regulated only indirectly if used in an AI system that fell into prohibited, high-risk, or transparency categories. | GPAI model providers must maintain technical documentation, provide downstream information, implement copyright compliance policy, and publish a training-content summary. |
| Systemic-risk tier | No equivalent tier. | Creates enhanced obligations for GPAI models with “systemic risk,” including model evaluation, adversarial testing, systemic-risk assessment/mitigation, serious-incident reporting, and cybersecurity. |
| Open-source treatment | No GPAI-specific open-source carveout. | Some GPAI obligations are relaxed for free/open-source models, but not for GPAI models with systemic risk. |
| Governance/enforcement | National competent authorities and European AI Board architecture; no AI Office role for foundation models. | AI Office/Commission has central GPAI oversight; codes of practice and harmonised standards become compliance tools. |
| Third-country providers | Non-EU provider representative rules existed for AI systems in certain contexts. | Non-EU GPAI model providers must appoint an EU authorised representative before placing the model on the EU market. |

## 1. 2021 proposal: no standalone foundation-model regime

The 2021 Commission proposal was framed around **AI systems**, not models as independent upstream assets. Its explanatory memorandum says the proposal established harmonised rules for “the development, placement on the market and use of AI systems” following a “risk-based approach,” with high-risk AI systems subject to mandatory requirements and conformity assessment before market placement. **EU AI Act 2021 Commission Proposal, Explanatory Memorandum, section 1.1 / 5.2; Title III framework.**

The 2021 definitions also covered actors such as **provider, user, authorised representative, importer, distributor, operator**, and concepts such as placing on the market, intended purpose, training data, validation data, testing data, conformity assessment and post-market monitoring, but did **not** define “general-purpose AI model,” “foundation model,” “general-purpose AI system,” “systemic risk,” or “downstream provider” in the final-act sense. **EU AI Act 2021 Commission Proposal, Article 3 definitions.**

As a result, in 2021 a foundation model would have been captured only indirectly—for example, if it was part of a **high-risk AI system**. The proposal’s high-risk obligations focused on system-level controls such as data governance, technical documentation, record-keeping, transparency to users, human oversight, accuracy, robustness, cybersecurity, corrective action, incident/risk information, and cooperation with authorities. **EU AI Act 2021 Commission Proposal, Recitals 42–44; Articles 14–15; Articles 21–23.**

## 2. Final 2024 Act: GPAI models are expressly in scope

The final 2024 Act expressly states that it lays down “harmonised rules for the placing on the market of general-purpose AI models.” **Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, Article 1(2)(e).**

It also extends scope to providers placing **general-purpose AI models** on the EU market, irrespective of whether those providers are established in the EU or in a third country. **Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, Article 2(1)(a).**

The final Act defines a **general-purpose AI model** as an AI model trained with large amounts of data, including by self-supervision at scale, that displays significant generality, can competently perform a wide range of distinct tasks, and can be integrated into many downstream systems or applications, excluding models used only for research, development or prototyping before market placement. **Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, Article 3(63).**

It also defines “general-purpose AI system,” “systemic risk,” “high-impact capabilities,” and “downstream provider,” which are concepts absent from the 2021 proposal. **Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, Article 3(64)–(68).**

## 3. New baseline obligations for GPAI model providers

The final 2024 text imposes direct obligations on providers of GPAI models. They must:

- draw up and keep up-to-date **technical documentation** of the model, including training and testing process and evaluation results; **Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, Article 53(1)(a), Annex XI.**
- provide information and documentation to downstream AI-system providers so they can understand the model’s capabilities and limitations and comply with their own AI Act obligations; **Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, Article 53(1)(b), Annex XII.**
- put in place a policy to comply with EU copyright law, including rights reservations under the DSM Directive text-and-data-mining framework; **Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, Article 53(1)(c).**
- publish a sufficiently detailed summary of the content used for training, using a template provided by the AI Office; **Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, Article 53(1)(d).**

None of these model-level obligations existed in the 2021 Commission proposal.

## 4. New enhanced obligations for GPAI models with systemic risk

The final Act creates a higher tier for **general-purpose AI models with systemic risk**. “Systemic risk” is defined as a risk specific to the high-impact capabilities of GPAI models that can significantly affect the EU market or cause reasonably foreseeable negative effects on public health, safety, public security, fundamental rights, or society as a whole, and that can propagate at scale across the value chain. **Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, Article 3(65).**

For GPAI models with systemic risk, providers must additionally:

- perform model evaluation using standardised protocols and tools, including adversarial testing; **Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, Article 55(1)(a).**
- assess and mitigate systemic risks at Union level; **Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, Article 55(1)(b).**
- track, document and report serious incidents and corrective measures to the AI Office and, where appropriate, national authorities; **Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, Article 55(1)(c).**
- ensure adequate cybersecurity protection for the model and its physical infrastructure; **Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, Article 55(1)(d).**

The Commission may designate a GPAI model as presenting systemic risk, including based on criteria in Annex XIII, and must maintain a public list of GPAI models with systemic risk, subject to protection of IP, confidential business information and trade secrets. **Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, Article 51(4)–(6), Annex XIII.**

This is a major expansion from the 2021 proposal, which had no equivalent systemic-risk model tier.

## 5. Open-source treatment added in the final Act

The final text creates a limited exemption for GPAI models released under a free and open-source licence where access, use, modification and distribution are allowed and the model parameters, weights, architecture information and usage information are publicly available. For such models, the Article 53(1)(a) technical-documentation and Article 53(1)(b) downstream-documentation duties do not apply. **Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, Article 53(2).**

However, that exemption does **not** apply to GPAI models with systemic risk. **Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, Article 53(2).**

The 2021 Commission proposal had no comparable GPAI-specific open-source model carveout.

## 6. New EU representative requirement for non-EU GPAI providers

The final Act requires providers of GPAI models established in third countries to appoint an EU-established authorised representative before placing a GPAI model on the Union market. **Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, Article 54(1).**

The 2021 proposal had authorised-representative obligations for providers of AI systems in the market-access framework, but not a dedicated third-country GPAI-model obligation because GPAI models were not a standalone regulated object. **EU AI Act 2021 Commission Proposal, Article 25; Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, Article 54.**

## 7. Codes of practice and AI Office oversight added for GPAI

The final Act introduces codes of practice to support compliance with GPAI obligations, especially Articles 53 and 55. The AI Office is tasked with encouraging and facilitating codes of practice, and those codes are expected to cover matters such as keeping GPAI documentation current, the level of detail for training-content summaries, systemic-risk identification, and systemic-risk management. **Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, Article 56(1)–(2).**

Providers may rely on approved codes of practice until harmonised standards are available; once harmonised standards exist, compliance with them can create a presumption of conformity for the covered obligations. **Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, Articles 53(4), 55(2), 56.**

The 2021 Commission proposal had a European Artificial Intelligence Board and national supervisory authorities, but no AI Office-centered GPAI compliance mechanism because GPAI models were not separately regulated. **EU AI Act 2021 Commission Proposal, Title VI; Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, Article 56.**

## Bottom line

The 2021 proposal regulated **AI applications/systems**, especially high-risk systems. It did not impose direct, upstream obligations on foundation-model developers merely because they developed or supplied a broadly capable model. The final 2024 Act adds a dedicated **general-purpose AI model regime**, with baseline documentation, downstream-transparency, copyright and training-summary obligations, plus stricter duties for models with systemic risk, including evaluation, adversarial testing, incident reporting, systemic-risk mitigation and cybersecurity.

scores.judge_rationale: The answer fully and accurately captures the key change from no standalone GPAI regime in 2021 to a dedicated Title VIIIa chapter with baseline and systemic-risk tier obligations in 2024, with extensive and precise citations to the correct regulation and sections including Article 53, Article 55, and related provisions of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689.

question.question: What are the most significant differences between the 1995 EU Data Protection Directive (95/46/EC) and the 2018 GDPR for organisations processing personal data?
question.expected_answer: Key differences: (1) Regulation vs Directive — GDPR is directly applicable across the EU, not requiring national transposition; (2) extraterritorial scope — GDPR applies to non-EU controllers offering goods/services to or monitoring EU data subjects; (3) explicit accountability — Articles 5(2), 24, 30 require demonstrable compliance and records of processing; (4) DPO obligation for certain entities (Article 37); (5) DPIA requirement (Article 35); (6) breach notification (Articles 33-34); (7) much higher fines (up to 4% of global turnover or €20M); (8) new/expanded data-subject rights (erasure, portability, automated-decision objection); (9) explicit data-protection-by-design (Article 25).

output.answer:
Below are the most significant practical differences for organisations processing personal data. The GDPR is formally Regulation (EU) 2016/679, adopted in 2016 and applicable from 25 May 2018; it repealed Directive 95/46/EC. *(GDPR Arts. 94, 99).*

| Area | Directive 95/46/EC position | GDPR position | Practical impact for organisations |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Legal form and harmonisation** | The 1995 instrument was a **Directive**, so Member States had to transpose it into national law, creating implementation differences across the EU. *(Directive 95/46/EC, Arts. 1, 32).* | The GDPR is a **Regulation**, laying down directly applicable rules across the EU. *(GDPR Art. 1; Art. 99).* | Multinational organisations moved from managing many national implementations to a more uniform EU-wide compliance framework, though Member State derogations still exist in some areas. |
| **Territorial reach** | The Directive focused mainly on processing in the context of an EU establishment, and in some cases use of “equipment” in a Member State. *(Directive 95/46/EC, Art. 4).* | The GDPR applies to EU-established controllers/processors and also to non-EU organisations that offer goods/services to, or monitor the behaviour of, individuals in the EU. *(GDPR Art. 3).* | Many non-EU businesses became directly subject to EU data protection law, especially online services, adtech, SaaS, and e-commerce providers targeting EU users. |
| **Accountability obligation** | The Directive contained data protection principles and required controllers to ensure compliance with them. *(Directive 95/46/EC, Art. 6(2)).* | The GDPR expressly requires controllers to be responsible for and **able to demonstrate** compliance. *(GDPR Art. 5(2); Art. 24).* | Organisations need evidence: policies, records, risk assessments, contracts, training, audit trails, and governance—not just compliant behaviour. |
| **Records and notification model** | The Directive relied heavily on notification/registration with supervisory authorities, subject to exemptions. *(Directive 95/46/EC, Arts. 18–19).* | The GDPR largely replaces general notification with internal **records of processing activities** and on-demand production to regulators. *(GDPR Art. 30).* | Organisations must maintain data maps/ROPA records, including purposes, categories of data subjects and data, recipients, transfers, retention periods, and security measures. |
| **Processor obligations** | The Directive placed most direct legal obligations on controllers; processors were mainly regulated through controller-processor contracts and security duties. *(Directive 95/46/EC, Art. 17).* | The GDPR imposes direct statutory duties on processors, including processing only on documented instructions, sub-processor controls, assistance duties, security duties, records, breach notification to controllers, and potential liability. *(GDPR Arts. 28–30, 32–33, 82–83).* | Vendors, cloud providers, payroll processors, SaaS providers, and other processors face direct regulatory exposure, not just contractual exposure. |
| **Data protection by design and default** | The Directive required appropriate security measures but did not contain an express “privacy by design/default” obligation. *(Directive 95/46/EC, Art. 17).* | The GDPR requires controllers to implement data protection by design and by default, including measures such as data minimisation and limiting default accessibility. *(GDPR Art. 25).* | Privacy requirements must be built into products, systems, workflows, access controls, and default settings from the design stage. |
| **Risk-based compliance: DPIAs and prior consultation** | The Directive used “prior checking” by supervisory authorities for processing likely to present specific risks. *(Directive 95/46/EC, Art. 20).* | The GDPR requires **data protection impact assessments** for processing likely to result in high risk and prior consultation where residual high risk remains. *(GDPR Arts. 35–36).* | Organisations must run structured privacy risk assessments for high-risk processing, such as large-scale sensitive data processing, systematic monitoring, or certain profiling activities. |
| **Data Protection Officers** | The Directive did not impose a general EU-wide DPO requirement, though national laws could use DPOs as part of notification exemptions. *(Directive 95/46/EC, Arts. 18–20).* | The GDPR requires a DPO for public authorities, large-scale regular and systematic monitoring, or large-scale processing of special-category/criminal-offence data. *(GDPR Art. 37).* DPO independence, resources, and tasks are specified. *(GDPR Arts. 38–39).* | Many organisations must appoint, empower, and protect an independent privacy officer with monitoring, advisory, and regulator-contact responsibilities. |
| **Breach notification** | The Directive had a general security obligation but no general EU-wide personal data breach notification duty for all controllers. *(Directive 95/46/EC, Art. 17).* | The GDPR requires notification to the supervisory authority without undue delay and, where feasible, within 72 hours, unless the breach is unlikely to risk individuals’ rights and freedoms; processors must notify controllers without undue delay. *(GDPR Art. 33).* High-risk breaches must also be communicated to affected individuals. *(GDPR Art. 34).* | Organisations need breach detection, escalation, investigation, documentation, regulator notification, and data-subject communication processes. |
| **Security requirements** | The Directive required appropriate technical and organisational security measures against accidental or unlawful destruction, loss, alteration, unauthorised disclosure, or access. *(Directive 95/46/EC, Art. 17).* | The GDPR retains the risk-based security duty and gives more concrete examples: pseudonymisation, encryption, confidentiality/integrity/availability/resilience, restoration capability, and regular testing. *(GDPR Art. 32).* | Security programs must be risk-based and demonstrable, with documented controls, testing, resilience, and incident response. |
| **Data subject rights** | The Directive provided rights of information, access, rectification, erasure/blocking, objection, and safeguards for automated decisions. *(Directive 95/46/EC, Arts. 10–12, 14–15).* | The GDPR expands and operationalises rights: transparent information, access, rectification, erasure/right to be forgotten, restriction, portability, objection, and rights concerning automated decision-making including profiling. *(GDPR Arts. 12–22).* | Organisations need mature request-handling processes, identity verification, response deadlines, portability mechanisms, deletion workflows, and profiling/automated-decision controls. |
| **Data portability** | The Directive did not contain a standalone right to data portability. *(Directive 95/46/EC, Arts. 12–15).* | The GDPR gives individuals the right to receive certain personal data in a structured, commonly used, machine-readable format and, where technically feasible, transmit it to another controller. *(GDPR Art. 20).* | Consumer platforms, apps, financial services, health tech, and SaaS providers may need export and transfer functionality. |
| **Consent standard and consent management** | The Directive defined consent as freely given, specific, and informed. *(Directive 95/46/EC, Art. 2(h)).* | The GDPR requires consent to be freely given, specific, informed, and unambiguous, and imposes conditions for proving consent and allowing withdrawal. *(GDPR Arts. 4(11), 7).* | Organisations need auditable consent records, clear affirmative opt-in mechanisms where consent is used, and easy withdrawal processes. |
| **Special categories and modern data types** | The Directive restricted processing of sensitive categories such as racial or ethnic origin, political opinions, religious or philosophical beliefs, trade-union membership, and health or sex-life data. *(Directive 95/46/EC, Art. 8).* | The GDPR retains special-category controls and expressly includes genetic data and biometric data used for unique identification. *(GDPR Arts. 4, 9).* | Organisations using biometrics, genetic data, health analytics, or identity verification technologies face clearer and often stricter obligations. |
| **International transfers** | The Directive allowed third-country transfers based on adequacy, derogations, or safeguards such as contractual clauses. *(Directive 95/46/EC, Arts. 25–26).* | The GDPR preserves the transfer framework but makes it more detailed, covering adequacy, appropriate safeguards, binding corporate rules, standard clauses, codes of conduct, certification, derogations, and onward-transfer protection. *(GDPR Arts. 44–49).* | Organisations need documented transfer mechanisms and must ensure the GDPR level of protection is not undermined when data leaves the EEA. |
| **Fines and enforcement exposure** | The Directive required Member States to provide sanctions but did not set EU-wide maximum administrative fine levels. *(Directive 95/46/EC, Art. 24).* | The GDPR creates harmonised administrative fine tiers: up to €10 million or 2% of worldwide annual turnover for certain infringements, and up to €20 million or 4% for more serious infringements. *(GDPR Art. 83).* | GDPR significantly increased financial and regulatory risk, making privacy compliance a board-level issue. |
| **Compensation and liability** | The Directive provided a right to compensation for damage caused by unlawful processing. *(Directive 95/46/EC, Art. 23).* | The GDPR provides compensation for material or non-material damage and expressly addresses controller and processor liability, including joint and several liability in certain cases. *(GDPR Art. 82).* | Organisations face broader litigation and damages exposure, including for distress or non-material harm where recognised by courts. |

**In short:** the GDPR did not replace the Directive’s core principles—lawfulness, fairness, purpose limitation, data quality, security, and individual rights—but it made them more operational, more enforceable, more global in reach, and much more evidence-based. For organisations, the biggest shift is from “comply with data protection rules” to “prove, continuously, that the organisation has governed and risk-managed its processing.”

scores.judge_rationale: The candidate answer comprehensively covers all key differences from the reference (regulation vs directive, extraterritoriality, accountability, DPO, DPIA, breach notification, fines, data subject rights including portability and erasure, data protection by design) with accurate and specific citations to the expected GDPR articles (3, 5, 25, 30, 33-35, 37, 83) plus additional relevant articles, while also correctly citing corresponding Directive provisions for comparative context.

question.question: Did the 2022 update to the SOC 2 Trust Services Criteria (the 'Points of Focus' update) change the certifiable criteria themselves, or only the guidance? Summarise.
question.expected_answer: The 2022 update primarily revised the 'points of focus' that accompany the criteria — i.e., the implementation guidance — without changing the criteria language itself for the most part. Material refinements were aimed at supply-chain risk, considering risks from environmental and emerging threats, communication of confidentiality commitments, and clearer treatment of system change management. Auditors continue to opine against the criteria; the points of focus inform how controls are evaluated.

output.answer:
No. The 2022 update did **not** change the certifiable SOC 2 Trust Services Criteria themselves. It updated only the **Points of Focus** associated with certain criteria.

Summary:

- The current document is still titled **“2017 Trust Services Criteria for Security, Availability, Processing Integrity, Confidentiality, and Privacy (With Revised Points of Focus — 2022)”**, indicating that the underlying criteria remain the 2017 TSC, while the 2022 change concerns revised Points of Focus. **SOC 2, TSP Section 100, Notice to Readers / Revisions in This Version**.
- The “Revisions in This Version” section states that the version was modified to reflect **“new points of focus and edits to extant points of focus”** relevant to certain trust services criteria. It does not say the criteria themselves were changed. **SOC 2, TSP Section 100, Revisions in This Version**.
- Points of Focus are described as representing **important characteristics of the criteria** and as potentially assisting management and practitioners in evaluating whether controls are suitably designed and operating effectively. They are guidance/supporting considerations, not the criteria on which the opinion is ultimately based. **SOC 2, TSP Section 100, Revisions in This Version; Background ¶.04**.
- SOC 2 examination opinions are expressed on whether controls are suitably designed and, for Type 2, operating effectively to achieve commitments and system requirements **based on the applicable trust services criteria**. **SOC 2, Description Criteria / SOC 2 examination discussion ¶.03**.
- For each trust services category in scope, the complete set consists of the applicable **criteria**—common criteria plus any category-specific criteria—not the Points of Focus. **SOC 2, TSP Section 100 ¶.09–.11**.

Bottom line: the 2022 update changed the **guidance/illustrative Points of Focus**, not the **certifiable Trust Services Criteria** used as the basis for SOC 2 reporting.

scores.judge_rationale: The candidate answer is fully correct in stating the 2022 update changed only Points of Focus (guidance) not the certifiable criteria themselves, and provides precise citations to SOC 2 TSP Section 100 including the document title, Revisions in This Version, and relevant paragraphs that directly support the answer.

question.question: How has SR 11-7 guidance on ongoing model monitoring evolved between the 2011 original and the 2026 SR 26-2 revision, particularly for AI/ML models?
question.expected_answer: The 2011 SR 11-7 emphasised periodic outcomes analysis and back-testing for static statistical models, with monitoring frequency tied to model risk-tier. SR 26-2 (2026) explicitly extends monitoring to AI/ML: continuous monitoring of distributional drift, performance decay, fairness/bias metrics, and emergent behaviour; explicit treatment of self-learning systems with retraining controls; vendor-AI-model monitoring obligations; and tighter governance over model changes via continuous-deployment pipelines. The 2026 revision treats the model lifecycle as continuous rather than periodic.

output.answer:
SR 11-7’s treatment of ongoing model monitoring has evolved from a **general validation activity** in the 2011 guidance into a more explicitly **risk-based, lifecycle-oriented monitoring expectation** in the 2026 SR 26-2 revision, with new scoping language for AI/ML.

| Topic | 2011 SR 11-7 original | 2026 SR 26-2 / revised model risk guidance | Practical effect for AI/ML models |
|---|---|---|---|
| Role of ongoing monitoring | Treated as one of the core components of model validation, alongside conceptual soundness and outcomes analysis. Monitoring was intended to confirm that the model remained properly implemented, used as intended, and performing as expected. **Citation: SR 11-7 (2011), Model Validation — Ongoing Monitoring.** | Reframed under **“Model Validation and Monitoring”** as part of a broader lifecycle process. Validation should identify limitations, errors, deterioration, and whether corrective action is warranted. **Citation: SR 26-2 / revised SR 11-7 (2026), Section V, Model Validation and Monitoring.** | AI/ML monitoring is no longer just periodic validation hygiene; it is part of lifecycle risk management from development through use and deterioration response. |
| Triggers for monitoring attention | 2011 focused on whether the model continued to operate as intended and whether changes in implementation, use, inputs, or performance required review. **Citation: SR 11-7 (2011), Model Validation — Ongoing Monitoring.** | 2026 expressly says ongoing monitoring evaluates whether a model is performing as expected given changes in **products, exposures, activities, clients, data relevance, or market conditions**. **Citation: SR 26-2 / revised SR 11-7 (2026), Section V, Ongoing Model Monitoring.** | This is more directly relevant to ML drift: changes in customer populations, data relevance, market regime, or business use become explicit monitoring triggers. |
| Response to deterioration | 2011 expected monitoring and outcomes analysis to identify performance issues and support changes such as adjustment or redevelopment. **Citation: SR 11-7 (2011), Model Validation — Ongoing Monitoring; Outcomes Analysis.** | 2026 states that a model that no longer performs as expected may warrant **overlays, adjustment, or redevelopment**, depending on the organization’s model risk management policy for model deterioration. **Citation: SR 26-2 / revised SR 11-7 (2026), Section V, Ongoing Model Monitoring.** | The 2026 language is more operational: firms should define deterioration thresholds and response paths, including overlays as interim risk mitigants. |
| Monitoring of limitations | 2011 emphasized identifying model limitations through validation and monitoring. **Citation: SR 11-7 (2011), Model Validation.** | 2026 says an effective monitoring plan may include regularly assessing model limitations **at development and over time**, plus procedures for responding to issues before and after approval for use. **Citation: SR 26-2 / revised SR 11-7 (2026), Section V, Ongoing Model Monitoring.** | For AI/ML, limitations such as training-data representativeness, unstable features, population drift, or weak performance in subsegments should be monitored throughout use, not only at initial validation. |
